anchor.title: Ahmad Shah Durrani
anchor.text: In 1747 Afghan leaders choose Ahmad Shah Durrani as ruler at Kandahar. His conquests create the Durrani Empire, commonly treated as a major foundation of the modern Afghan state, though its borders and institutions differ greatly from those of modern Afghanistan.

meanwhile.title: Sugar and the enslaved majority
meanwhile.text: Planters carve the valleys into sugar estates worked by enslaved Africans, shipped in through the Middle Passage until they vastly outnumber the whites. Cane, rum and molasses make a few families rich. The labor that makes them rich is coerced, brutal and lethal, and the island's people are overwhelmingly the descendants of the enslaved.

meanwhile.title: Nutmeg makes the Isle of Spice
meanwhile.text: Nutmeg trees, carried from the East Indies, take to Grenada's volcanic soil. Within a lifetime the island becomes a major global nutmeg producer, the fruit later stamped on its flag. Split nutmeg and its red lace of mace still dry in the Gouyave sheds, the reason Grenada is called the Isle of Spice.

meanwhile.title: Potosí
meanwhile.text: Potosí becomes one of the Spanish Empire's great silver-mining centers. From 1573 the colonial mita requires more than 200 Indigenous communities to send roughly one-seventh of their adult men for rotating labor service. Mining, mercury exposure, coercion and disease impose severe human costs, but later claims of eight million deaths are not a reliable demographic estimate.

meanwhile.title: French conquest of Algeria
meanwhile.text: During the French conquest, troops under Colonel Aimable Pélissier seal members of the Ouled Riah inside caves in the Dahra and kill hundreds by smoke and fire. The wider conquest brings warfare, displacement, famine and disease and causes severe population loss.

meanwhile.title: The Baku Khanate
meanwhile.text: As central authority collapses, Baku emerges as a self-governing khanate centered on its walled port. Its rulers draw revenue from Caspian trade and the oil-bearing lands of Absheron.

meanwhile.title: Declared a neutral island
meanwhile.text: In the mid-eighteenth century Britain and France continue to treat Dominica as one of the so-called neutral islands, where neither power has established undisputed sovereignty. The 1748 European peace does not end local competition, and both French settlement and Kalinago resistance continue.
